subject: chemistry
title: Ligand substitution and stability constants
key_idea: In ligand substitution one ligand in a complex is swapped for another, often with a colour change. Bidentate and multidentate ligands replace monodentate ones because the entropy of the system rises: this is the chelate effect.

blocks.text: Ligands in a complex can be swapped for others. Whether the coordination number changes depends on the size and charge of the ligands.

items: H₂O and NH₃ are similar in size and both uncharged. Swapping them does **not** change the coordination number.
Cl⁻ is larger than H₂O and NH₃ and is charged. Swapping H₂O for Cl⁻ can change the coordination number from 6 to 4.
Substitution may be incomplete: some H₂O ligands remain.
With a little ammonia, [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ first gives a pale blue precipitate of Cu(OH)₂(H₂O)₄. Excess ammonia then dissolves it to give the deep blue solution.
Cl⁻ replaces H₂O only when the chloride ion concentration is high, for example in concentrated hydrochloric acid. Adding water reverses the change.
Ligand exchange can also happen with Co²⁺ and NH₃, and with Fe³⁺ and Cl⁻.
H₂O to NH₃: same coordination number. H₂O to Cl⁻: coordination number can fall from 6 to 4.
Ligand substitution usually changes the colour.
Write substitution equations with complexed formulae and ⇌.

blocks.text: Haemoglobin shows ligand substitution in the body.

items: Haem is an iron(II) complex with a multidentate ligand. You need not know its structure.
Oxygen forms a coordinate bond to Fe²⁺ in haemoglobin. This lets oxygen be carried round the blood.
Oxygen is released where it is needed, because the bond is weak enough to break.
Carbon monoxide is toxic because it replaces the oxygen on Fe²⁺, in a ligand substitution.
CO binds more strongly than O₂ and does not easily leave, so the blood can no longer carry oxygen.
Oxygen bonds reversibly to Fe²⁺ in haemoglobin.
CO replaces O₂ by ligand exchange.
CO binds more strongly, so oxygen transport is blocked.

blocks.text: Bidentate and multidentate ligands replace monodentate ligands, and the new complex is more stable. This is the **chelate effect**.

blocks.label: Example: three bidentate ligands replace six water molecules
where: 4 particles on the left, 7 on the right.

items: The number of particles rises from 4 to 7, so there is a large positive increase in the entropy of the system (ΔS).
The bonds broken (Ni–O) and made (Ni–N) are similar in strength, so the enthalpy change is close to zero.
Free energy change ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is therefore negative, because ΔS is positive. The reaction is feasible and the products are favoured.
EDTA⁴⁻ is multidentate, so one ion replaces six water molecules and gives a very large entropy gain.
Chelate effect: bidentate or multidentate ligands replace monodentate ones.
More particles are formed, so entropy rises.
ΔH is about zero, so the balance of enthalpy and entropy favours the product.

checks.q: Describe what you see when concentrated hydrochloric acid is added to aqueous copper(II) sulfate, and write the equation.
checks.a: The pale blue solution turns yellow-green. [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4Cl⁻ ⇌ [CuCl₄]²⁻ + 6H₂O.

checks.q: Explain why carbon monoxide is toxic.
checks.a: CO is a ligand that forms a coordinate bond to Fe²⁺ in haemoglobin. It replaces oxygen and binds more strongly, so oxygen can no longer be transported in the blood.

checks.q: Explain, in terms of entropy, why replacing six H₂O ligands with three bidentate ligands gives a more stable complex.
checks.a: The number of particles increases from 4 to 7, so ΔS (system) is large and positive. ΔH is about zero, so ΔG is negative and the more stable complex is formed.

items: Learn the substitution and colour changes for [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ and [CuCl₄]²⁻ from [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺, and for [Cr(NH₃)₆]³⁺ from [Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺.
Use complexed formulae in substitution equations.
Explain the importance of iron in haemoglobin, including ligand substitution involving O₂ and CO.
Ligand exchange in copper(II) goes via Cu(OH)₂(H₂O)₄ to [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺, and to [CuCl₄]²⁻. In cobalt(II), [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ gives [CoCl₄]²⁻.
Replacing small, uncharged ligands (H₂O) with larger, charged ligands (Cl⁻) can change the coordination number.
The stability of complexes with bidentate and multidentate ligands is explained by a large positive increase in ΔS of the system.
Examples of exchange without change of coordination number: Co²⁺ and Cu²⁺ with H₂O and NH₃.
Examples of exchange of H₂O by Cl⁻ involving a change of coordination number: Co²⁺, Cu²⁺ and Fe³⁺.
Explain the chelate effect in terms of the balance between the entropy and enthalpy change in these reactions.
Explain ligand exchange qualitatively for copper(II) and cobalt(II) with water, ammonia, hydroxide and chloride ligands.
Use these complexes as examples of ligand exchange changing the colour observed.
Write Kstab expressions without [H₂O] and use them in calculations, including finding an unknown equilibrium concentration.
Explain ligand exchange in terms of Kstab: the new complex has a larger Kstab than the one it replaces.

blocks.text: The stability constant measures how far the formation of a complex goes.

items.meaning: The equilibrium constant for the formation of a complex ion in a solvent from its constituent ions or molecules.

blocks.label: Kstab for the silver ammine complex
where: Concentrations are equilibrium concentrations in mol dm⁻³.

diagram.alt: Calculate a stability constant from equilibrium concentrations.
diagram.question: At equilibrium, a solution has [[Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺] = {c} mol dm⁻³, [Ag⁺] = {a} × 10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³ and [NH₃] = {n} mol dm⁻³. Calculate Kstab for Ag⁺ + 2NH₃ ⇌ [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ in mol⁻² dm⁶.

items: A **large** Kstab means the equilibrium lies far to the right: a stable complex.
A ligand that forms a complex with a larger Kstab replaces one with a smaller Kstab.
Work out the units from the expression. Divide the units of the top by the units of the bottom.
Kstab is the equilibrium constant for forming the complex. Leave out [H₂O].
Large Kstab: stable complex.
Ligand exchange goes towards the complex with the larger Kstab.
